```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 8 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Integrals</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">8.1</span> Volume Forms and Orientation</h1></header>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Given a smooth manifold <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})_d\)</span>, a <strong>volume form</strong> is a <span class="math inline">\((0,d)\)</span>-tensor field  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \Omega : \underbrace{\Gamma T\mathcal{M} \times \dots \times \Gamma T\mathcal{M}}_{d\text{-times}}
            &amp;\xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \dots \\ \sim}} C^\infty(\mathcal{M}) \\
            \big( \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(d)} \big) &amp;\longmapsto \Omega\big( \mathcal{X}_{(1)}, \dots, \mathcal{X}_{(d)} \big),
        \end{align*}</span>  satisfying:</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p><em>Non-vanishing:</em> <span class="math inline">\(\Omega_p \neq 0\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(p \in \mathcal{M}\)</span>;</p></li>
<li><p><em>Total antisymmetry:</em> exchanging any two arguments flips the sign,  <span class="math display">\[
                    \Omega\big( \dots, \underbrace{\mathcal{X}_{(a)}}_{a\text{-th}}, \dots, \underbrace{\mathcal{X}_{(b)}}_{b\text{-th}}, \dots \big)
                    = - \Omega\big( \dots, \underbrace{\mathcal{X}_{(b)}}_{a\text{-th}}, \dots, \underbrace{\mathcal{X}_{(a)}}_{b\text{-th}}, \dots \big)
                    \qquad \forall \, a \neq b \in \{1, \dots, d\} .
                \]</span></p></li>
</ol></li>
<li><p>The <span class="math inline">\(d\)</span>-dimensional <strong>Levi-Civita symbol</strong> is the array <span class="math inline">\(\varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} = \varepsilon^{i_1 \dots i_d}\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(i_1, \dots, i_d \in \{1, \dots, d\}\)</span>, fixed by <span class="math inline">\(\varepsilon_{1 \dots d} = 1\)</span> and total antisymmetry, <span class="math inline">\(\varepsilon_{\dots i_a \dots i_b \dots} = - \varepsilon_{\dots i_b \dots i_a \dots}\)</span><sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-3" id="fnref-3" aria-label="Footnote 3">3</a></sup>. It vanishes if two indices coincide (exchanging them gives <span class="math inline">\(\varepsilon = -\varepsilon\)</span>), and otherwise equals the sign of the permutation <span class="math inline">\((i_1, \dots, i_d)\)</span> of <span class="math inline">\((1, \dots, d)\)</span>. For a totally antisymmetric array <span class="math inline">\(T_{i_1 \dots i_d}\)</span> and a matrix <span class="math inline">\(T^i_j\)</span> (we’ll employ these properties afterwards)<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-4" id="fnref-4" aria-label="Footnote 4">4</a></sup>:  <span class="math display">\[
            \underbrace{T_{i_1 \dots i_d} = \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, T_{1 \dots d}}_{\text{(a)}},
            \qquad
            \underbrace{\det \big( T^i_j \big) = \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, T^{i_1}_1 \cdots T^{i_d}_d}_{\text{(b)}},
            \qquad
            \underbrace{\varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, T^{i_1}_{j_1} \cdots T^{i_d}_{j_d} = \det \big( T^i_j \big) \, \varepsilon_{j_1 \dots j_d}}_{\text{(c)}} .
        \]</span></p></li>
<li><p>In a chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>, the components of a volume form, <span class="math inline">\((\Omega_\mathscr{X})_{i_1 \dots i_d} \coloneqq \Omega\big( \partial x_{i_1}, \dots, \partial x_{i_d} \big) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U})\)</span>, form a totally antisymmetric array:  <span class="math display">\[
            (\Omega_\mathscr{X})_{i_1 \dots i_d} = \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, \omega_\mathscr{X} ,
            \qquad
            \omega_\mathscr{X} \coloneqq (\Omega_\mathscr{X})_{1 \dots d} = \Omega\big( \partial x_1, \dots, \partial x_d \big) \in C^\infty(\mathcal{U}) .
        \]</span>  The function <span class="math inline">\(\omega_\mathscr{X}\)</span> is the <strong>scalar density</strong> of <span class="math inline">\(\Omega\)</span> w.r.t. <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>.  As every component is <span class="math inline">\(\pm \omega_\mathscr{X}\)</span> or <span class="math inline">\(0\)</span>, the non-vanishing condition reads <span class="math inline">\(\omega_\mathscr{X}(p) \neq 0\, \forall p \in \mathcal{U}\)</span>. Under a change of chart, on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}\)</span>,  <span class="math display" id="eq_scalar_density_transformation">\begin{align}
            \omega_\mathscr{Y}
            &amp;\coloneqq \Omega\big( \partial y_1, \dots, \partial y_d \big)
            =
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^1} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_d}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^d} \;
            \Omega\big( \partial x_{i_1}, \dots, \partial x_{i_d} \big)
            = \tag{8.1}\\
            &amp;=
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^1} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_d}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^d} \;
            (\Omega_\mathscr{X})_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, =
            \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_1}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^1} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^{i_d}}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^d}
            \, \varepsilon_{i_1 \dots i_d} \, \omega_\mathscr{X}
            \overset{(c)}{=}
            \det \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right) \omega_\mathscr{X}. \tag{8.2}
        \end{align}</span>  Therefore, under a change of basis, the scalar density  <span class="math inline">\(\omega_\mathscr{X}\)</span> picks up a Jacobian  determinant term.<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-5" id="fnref-5" aria-label="Footnote 5">5</a></sup> In particular, <span class="math inline">\(\omega_\mathscr{X}\)</span> is not a scalar field on <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span>: its values at a point depend on the chart.</p></li>
<li><p>Let <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A})_d\)</span> be a smooth manifold, with <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}\)</span> its maximal atlas. An atlas <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}^\uparrow \subseteq \mathcal{A}\)</span>, i.e. a set of charts whose domains cover <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span>, is an <strong>oriented atlas</strong> if all its Jacobian determinants are positive,  <span class="math display">\[
            \det \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)(p) &gt; 0
            \qquad \forall \, p \in \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V}, \quad \forall \, (\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}), (\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \in \mathcal{A}^\uparrow .
        \]</span>  The condition is symmetric in the two charts, since the two Jacobians are inverse matrices:  <span class="math display">\[
            \det \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \right) \, \det \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^k} \right)
            = \det \left( \frac{\partial \mathscr{X}^i}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j} \frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^j}{\partial \mathscr{X}^k} \right)
            = \det \big( \delta^i_k \big) = 1 .
        \]</span>  A smooth manifold is <strong>orientable</strong> if it admits an oriented atlas<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-6" id="fnref-6" aria-label="Footnote 6">6</a></sup>, and the triple <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}^\uparrow)\)</span> is then an <strong>oriented manifold</strong>.</p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-footnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-3"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-3" aria-label="Back to the text">3</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p><span class="math inline">\(\varepsilon\)</span> is a symbol, the same array in every chart, not the components of a tensor field. Its upper and lower versions have the same entries; the index position only allows them to enter the summation convention.</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-4"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-4" aria-label="Back to the text">4</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>(a) As for <span class="math inline">\(\varepsilon\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(T\)</span> vanishes on repeated indices, and each exchange of two indices flips its sign. (b) <span class="math inline">\(\det \big( T^i_j \big) = \sum_\sigma \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) \, T^{\sigma(1)}_1 \cdots T^{\sigma(d)}_d\)</span>, the terms with repeated indices dropping out of the sum over <span class="math inline">\(i_1, \dots, i_d\)</span>. (c) Relabelling <span class="math inline">\(i_a \leftrightarrow i_b\)</span> shows that the left-hand side is totally antisymmetric in <span class="math inline">\(j_1, \dots, j_d\)</span>; by (a) it equals <span class="math inline">\(\varepsilon_{j_1 \dots j_d}\)</span> times its value at <span class="math inline">\((1, \dots, d)\)</span>, which is <span class="math inline">\(\det \big( T^i_j \big)\)</span> by (b).</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-5"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-5" aria-label="Back to the text">5</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>Quantities that pick up a power  <span class="math inline">\(\det\big( \partial \mathscr{X}^i / \partial \mathscr{Y}^j \big)^w\)</span>  under a change of chart are often called densities of weight <span class="math inline">\(w\)</span>.  Defining what a density is, rather than how it transforms,  requires intoducing the frame bundle of <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span>  and the density bundles associated with it.  For this chapter the transformation law  is all that is needed, and <span class="math inline">\(\omega_\mathscr{X}\)</span> can be viewed simply as function on  <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U}\)</span> attached to each chart.</p></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-6"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-6" aria-label="Back to the text">6</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>Orientability is a global property: every chart domain, equipped with its single chart, is trivially oriented. The standard example of a non-orientable manifold is the Möbius strip.</p></div></div></div>
```
